chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: The Onyx Club year and the sudden fame of 1937-38
summary: She was at the Onyx from July to December, then midtown and the Cotton Club; she overcame hurdles quickly.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I was just thinking a few minutes ago while we were off tape, while you were occupied doing something else, that, here you came to New York, you were - first you started to break into a white dominated industry, the music business, the entertainment field, a male dominated business largely, almost entirely, and I think you also mentioned to me a couple of sessions ago that people came from Harlem would be more likely to have connections into some kind of network that was associated with show business and the world of entertainment than for someone who came from out of town, as you did. You had three ways in which you were an outsider almost.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
To overcome all those hurdles all at once.

Yes, I had been downtown at the Onyx I would say from July till December and the first chance I got to appear in Harlem was at a Christmas show that they had at the Apollo Theatre. It was a benefit performance, of course, and I came up to the Apollo Theatre from the Onyx Club and Noble Sissle Band was on stage and I did 'Lock Loman' of course. And that was the first time it had been heard in Harlem and they liked it. So I had broken the ice. But, when you consider that most of the clubs, the black performers and bands were more or less established in Harlem, the Apollo Theatre, and the other theatres and most of the clubs, I was indeed an outsider. Also, I don't know whether, I really don't know whether there were any barriers to performers from Harlem working downtown or not. Of course in 1938 the Cotton Club moved downtown. That was the first show, I would say, to appear down in the Broadway area that was considered a predominately black production, although I'm sure there had been performers

in musical productions in the mid-town area. But it was a new thing in 1938. And of course, the Cotton Club didn't last downtown. I would think that the tourist who came to New York and had heard about the Cotton Club would have preferred to go to the Cotton Club than Harlem because downtown there were other places to go and it didn't mean that much by comparison. The first few years the Cotton Club did very well. But after a few years it just didn't matter, they were just competing with other clubs. It didn't matter whether it was a black show or a white show or what.
Yes. You closed at the Cotton Club?

Okay, so anyway you went into the Onyx Club and you stayed there for about a year. I've got a copy from DownBeat, September '38 and here it says that after remaining at the Onyx Club for almost a year you, that's when you went out to Hollywood to do an engagement with Selznick?
